Yes. 

The ending feels entirely natural, purposeful, and earned because it gracefully resolves the central psychological conflict of the story while tying together all of its major motifs. 

Throughout the story, the recurring dream of the empty, sunlit flat represents the parts of himself Daniel had locked away and "put back in boxes" during his previous marriage to keep the peace. By finding the literal keys from his youth and sharing the cherished memory of canoeing with Isabel, Daniel finally brings those neglected parts of himself into his current life. The ending directly echoes earlier moments in the text—the "thin gold light" of the dream now falls on Isabel instead of an empty floor, the quiet moment with the heron mirrors the unspoken bond he had with his father, and the fading of the dream fulfills Isabel's earlier observation that "you never notice the last one." Every thread is given closure, leaving the reader with a deep sense of completion.
